title: AIADMK on the Brink: MLAs Revolt Against EPS
excerpt: A 30-strong rebel bloc led by C.V. Shanmugam challenges Edappadi Palaniswami's grip on Tamil Nadu's historic opposition party.
body:
On May 11, 2026, the opening day of Tamil Nadu's 17th Legislative Assembly, the AIADMK announced its own crisis to the world — not in a press release, but in the way its legislators walked through the door.

**What happened:**
The party's 47 MLAs arrived in two separate groups, with just 11 legislators walking in alongside former Chief Minister Edappadi K. Palaniswami, while a larger bloc of 36, led by senior leaders C.V. Shanmugam and S.P. Velumani, entered separately. Only 17 of the 47 MLAs signed a letter submitted to the Interim Speaker supporting Palaniswami as legislature party leader, leaving 30 legislators conspicuously absent from the endorsement.

**Why the revolt is happening:**
This defeat marks the fourth consecutive electoral setback for the party since Palaniswami took control of the AIADMK. Dissidents accuse EPS of taking 'unilateral decisions' and prioritising personal interest over party welfare following the AIADMK's drop to third place in the polls. Shanmugam and ally S.P. Velumani reportedly discussed a post-poll arrangement with Vijay's TVK when it was short of a majority, while EPS was said to be engaging in talks with the DMK. EPS is refusing to budge.

**What the anti-defection law means:**
India's anti-defection law requires at least two-thirds of a legislature party to support a split for MLAs to avoid disqualification — meaning the rebel faction needs 32 of AIADMK's 47 MLAs, and reports place them just two members short of that threshold. Some reports suggest the faction not aligned with EPS is willing to merge with Chief Minister Vijay's TVK.

**What to watch:**
Speculation is mounting that Shanmugam and his supporters might back Vijay on the floor test on May 13 — a vote that could formally fracture one of Tamil Nadu's oldest political institutions.
nri_angle: Tamil Americans with roots in Tamil Nadu are watching closely because the collapse of the AIADMK — the party that governed the state for decades under Jayalalithaa — would permanently redraw the political map of a state central to Dravidian identity and diaspora pride.
author: Diaspora Desk
